column2: The syllable Om is made of speech and is everything; therefore one should practise Om. It is "a", "u", and "m", with a half-measure.
Its three measures are the three Vedas, the worlds Bhur and the rest, the qualities; waking, dream and deep sleep; Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara.
In order: Pradyumna, Shri, Vasudeva — Om is all of these. The measureless, with its measures gone, is the cessation of duality: Shiva.
The sage who knows Om is the true sage, none other. The fourth measure, "gandhari", when used, is perceived at the head.
That is the fourth (turiya), the supreme Brahman, a light like a lamp in a pot. Thus a man should meditate on and constantly chant it, dwelling in the heart-lotus.
Om is the bow, the self is the arrow, Brahman is called the target. It should be pierced with care; one should become one with it like an arrow.
This is the one-syllable Brahman, this one syllable is supreme; knowing this one syllable, whatever one wishes, one obtains.
Its metre is the goddess Gayatri; the Inner Controller is held to be its seer; its deity is the Supreme Self; its application is for enjoyment and liberation.
Bhuh, to the Self of fire is the heart; "Bhuvah, to the Self of Prajapati" the head; "Svah, to the Self of the sun" the tuft; this is called the armour.
Om Bhur Bhuvah Svah is the armour; then "to the Self of truth" the weapon. Having placed these, one should worship Vishnu and chant for enjoyment and liberation.
One should offer sesame and ghee; everything is accomplished for a man. Whoever practises twelve thousand repetitions daily...
...in twelve months the Supreme Brahman shines forth for him. By ten million repetitions come the powers beginning with anima; by a hundred thousand, learning such as Sarasvata.
The sacrifice to Vishnu is threefold: Vedic, tantric, and mixed. One should worship Hari by one of the three according to desire.
He who worships by prostrating on the ground like a staff, with salutation, attains a state that is not reached even by a hundred sacrifices.
He who has supreme devotion to God, and as to God so to the teacher, to that great soul these teachings shine forth.
As one fills a skin with outer air, so one stays full; because of filling, it is called "puraka" (inhalation).
He neither exhales nor inhales the air, held within and outside; he stays motionless like a full pot — that is "kumbhaka" (retention).
The lowest, with one stroke, has twelve measures; the middle, with two strokes, has twenty-four measures.
The best, with three strokes, has thirty-six clap-measures; it produces sweat, trembling and shock; this is the best of the best.
From unconquered breath one cannot rise from the ground; hiccup, breathlessness and the like arise; when breath is conquered, the excretion of faeces and urine is reduced.
The results are health, swiftness, zeal, excellence of voice, strength and clear complexion, and the destruction of all faults.
Without chanting and meditation it is "agarbha"; with them it is "sagarbha". For conquering the senses one should practise the sagarbha form.
By knowledge and dispassion and the power of pranayama, having conquered the senses, everything is conquered.
The senses are all that: heaven and hell both. Restrained or let loose, they lead to heaven or to hell.
The body is called a chariot, the senses its horses, the mind is said to be the charioteer, and pranayama the whip (or goad).
The mind, held by the reins of knowledge and dispassion, gradually becomes steady, joined with pranayama alone.
One who drinks a drop of water from the tip of kusha grass month after month for a full hundred years — pranayama is equal to that.
When the senses, attached, have entered the ocean of objects, whoever draws them back and restrains them: this is called "pratyahara".
One should lift oneself by oneself, as one sinking in water; by the great force of the river of enjoyments, one should take refuge in the tree of knowledge.
Whether pure or impure, one should meditate on the Lord a hundred times, fixing Keshava in the mind at the end of the body's dwelling.
In the middle of the seat of the heart-lotus one should worship by the discipline of meditation. The sacrifice of meditation is supreme, pure, free of all faults.
Having sacrificed with it one attains liberation, not by outwardly pure sacrifices; being free from the fault of violence, it is the means of purifying the mind.
Therefore the sacrifice of meditation is supreme and gives the fruit of liberation. So, abandoning impure, impermanent outward means...
...and giving up the rites of sacrifice and the like, one should practise yoga intensely. The unmanifest, free of change, joined with the enjoyer and the enjoyed...
one should first contemplate in the heart, in order, the three qualities: cover tamas with rajas, and rajas with sattva.
One should meditate on the three circles: first black, then red, then white. The twenty-fifth principle, the Person, is beyond the qualities that are limiting conditions of sattva.
This is to be meditated on; abandoning what is impure, one should contemplate the pure. A divine lotus of lordship stands above the Person...
...twelve finger-breadths wide, pure, open, white; its stalk has eight parts, arising from the bulb at the navel.
Know its eight petals as the eight qualities beginning with anima; its pericarp and filaments, the stalk — knowledge and dispassion — are the best.
The bulb is the dharma of Vishnu: so one should contemplate the lotus. It is supreme, made of that dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and the lordship of Shiva.
Knowing the lotus-seat, one attains the end of all sorrow. In the middle of its pericarp, shaped like a pure lamp-flame...
...the thumb-sized, stainless Lord, Om, should be meditated on, in a form like a star, shaped like a kadamba bud.
Or one should meditate on the Lord seated in the lotus, shining everywhere with a net of rays, the Primal beyond Purusha.
One should meditate on and constantly chant the supreme imperishable Om; for steadying the mind, gross meditation is taught first, in order.
One who has become steady attains the subtle too. The stalk standing in the navel-bulb is ten finger-breadths long.
By the stalk, the eight-petalled lotus is twelve finger-breadths wide; with its pericarp and long filaments, it holds the discs of sun, moon and fire.
In the middle of the fire-disc stands Vishnu with conch, discus and mace, with lotus, four-armed; or Hari with eight arms.
Holding the Sharnga bow, rosary and bracelet, noose and goad, supreme, golden or white, with the Shrivatsa and the Kaustubha.
Wearing a garland of wild flowers and a golden necklace, with shining shark-shaped earrings, a crown bright with jewels, clothed in yellow, great.
Rich in all ornaments, as large or small as one wishes: "I am Brahman, the light-self, Vasudeva, liberated, Om."
Tired of meditation, one should chant the mantra; tired of chanting, one should meditate. For one joined to chanting and meditation, Vishnu is quickly pleased.

Sacrifices do not equal a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of chanting. Diseases, mental troubles and malign planets do not approach the one who chants. Enjoyment, liberation and victory over death are obtained by chanting.
With the channels, one should pierce the fearful, divine, auspicious trident-tip; from the big toe to the crown of the head it is encompassed by a circle of rays.
Streams going crosswise, downward and upward with great brilliance — the best of seekers should contemplate that, O great sage, until all...
...the body has become ash; then he should withdraw it into himself. Cold, phlegm and other faults, and sin, are destroyed, O twice-born.
He should recall the head, the syllable, and the throat facing downward; with unbroken thought he should meditate on the self in the elemental self again and again.
With streams that come from a cold, sprinkling mist and touch of spray, one should imagine the whole universe filled on earth.
From the Brahma-aperture, through the stirring, as far as the base-circle, going within the Sushumna, he should reach the dwelling made by the full moon...
...bathed in water of cold touch, of nectar form; the one tormented by hunger and thirst and exhausted...
should practise the Varuni concentration with the mantra, undisturbed, for contentment. The Varuni concentration is told; hear now the Aishani concentration.
In the sky, in the lotus made of Brahman, when prana and apana have dwindled, one should contemplate Vishnu's grace until thought has come to an end.
One should chant of the great state, everything; then the Lord is all-pervading — the half-moon, supreme, tranquil, without appearance, stainless.
Until one sees one's own pulsation-form from the teacher's mouth, the unreal appears real, and so does everything moving and unmoving.
When that supreme reality is seen, from Brahma down to the moving and unmoving, the knower, the means of knowledge and the known...
...and the imagining of the heart-lotus in meditation — all chanting, offerings and worship are like a mother's sweets. Or through the Vishnu mantra I shall teach the "amrita" concentration.
One should meditate on a lotus like the full moon, held in the grip of the strings; with effort one should imagine it at the head, with the brilliance of ten thousand moons.

A full disc in the sky, filled with the waves of Shiva; likewise one should meditate on the heart-lotus and recall one's own body in its middle. The practitioner becomes free of affliction through such concentrations.
Ether, wind, fire, water, earth and metals — these are the worlds, and this is the Self; therefore it includes the moving and unmoving.
As a potter makes a pot with clay, staff and wheel, or a builder a house with grass, clay and wood...
...so the Self, taking the organs, in those various wombs here, forms itself; the Self, together with the organs, emerges.
By karma, through fault and delusion and by desire alone, he is bound; by knowledge the soul is freed; by dharma the yogi is not subject to disease.
As a lamp stands through the union of wick, vessel and oil, so, seeing change as well, the life-breath is lost untimely.
Endless are his rays, who stands in the heart like a lamp: white, black, brown, blue, tawny, yellow and red.
One of these stands upward; by piercing the sun's disc and passing beyond the world of Brahma, by it one goes to the highest goal.
By the other hundred rays that stand upward, one obtains the abodes of the hosts of gods.
